text: Lesson twelve built IncidentUtils as a standalone class with no parent at all. Here's a more specific class that extends it — PriorityIncidentUtils — using the real ServiceNow inheritance pattern that most production code on a mature instance actually relies on, instead of duplicating logic across unrelated classes.

Object.extendsObject takes two arguments: the parent class, IncidentUtils, and an object literal holding the child's own methods. The result of that call becomes PriorityIncidentUtils' prototype, so the new class inherits every single method IncidentUtils already had — isHighPriority, getOpenDurationHours — and layers its own needsEscalation method on top, which checks both high priority and how long the incident has actually been open against a four-hour escalation threshold.

Notice the very first line inside the child's initialize: IncidentUtils.prototype.initialize.call, passing this. There's no super keyword anywhere in this pattern — instead, you explicitly reach into the parent class's own prototype, grab its initialize method, and call it with this bound to the current child instance. Skip that single line, and the parent's setup, like priorityThreshold, silently never runs at all, which only shows up much later, once some inherited method depending on it starts misbehaving in a way that's genuinely confusing to debug.

So when should a class actually extend another one, rather than standing alone? The real test, every time, is IS-A: PriorityIncidentUtils genuinely is an IncidentUtils, with escalation logic layered on top — a real, meaningful parent-child relationship with shared state and shared methods. When two classes merely happen to touch the same table, like one formatting incident numbers for a report and another routing incidents to assignment groups, forcing an inheritance relationship between them just to save a few lines creates a false dependency, where a change meant for one purpose can quietly break the other.

Object.extendsObject for the mechanics, calling super explicitly for the constructor chain, and the IS-A test for the decision itself — that's real inheritance in ServiceNow, done the way working developers actually do it. Next, the Script Includes Lab puts both the base class and the extended class together in one complete, worked build from start to finish.
